reading.rtitle: The Quarter That Changed the Rule
paras: Last year the credit team of a digital bank in Recife had the best quarter in its short history, and then it had the worst one. The two happened in a row, and nobody saw the second one coming.

In April they launched a new product for customers who had never borrowed before. Revenue rose in May, and it rose again in June. The team was young and it celebrated. The dashboard looked exactly like the plan, and the plan looked easy.

Then in August the numbers turned. The cohort that started in April reached its third payment, and a spike appeared in the default rate. It did not fall back. In September the bank wrote off more money in one month than it earned in the whole of June, and the write-off landed in the same week as the quarterly review.

The team did not argue about the model. They read the policy line by line, and they found the change: in March somebody loosened a rule to let more customers in, and nobody wrote down why. They tightened it again in October, they lost some growth, and they kept one habit from that quarter. Every change to the policy now carries a name, a date and a reason. That was the real milestone.
reading.source: A composite account of a Brazilian digital-bank credit desk, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how a digital bank chooses a new product.
To show how one quarter went from the best to the worst, and what the team changed because of it.
To argue that banks should never lend to first-time customers.

items.situation: Say what the team did in April, in one sentence.
tips: They launched a new product for first-time borrowers.
Regular verb: launch becomes launched, for every subject.

items.situation: Now say two things that happened in August and September.
tips: A spike appeared in the default rate, and it did not fall back.
In September the bank wrote off more than it earned in June. Note: write becomes wrote, not writed.

items.situation: Ask a question in the past about the March change.
tips: Did anybody write down the reason?
Not: Did anybody wrote. After did, the verb goes back to its base form.

items.situation: The text says the team did not argue about the model. Say what they did instead.
tips: They read the policy line by line.
Read in the past is spelled the same and sounds like red.

items.situation: Say what happened in one real quarter of your own.
tips: We tightened the policy and the rate dropped in two months.
We launched a new limit and revenue rose, and then the cohort turned.

items.situation: Ask me two questions in the past about my last quarter, one with did and one with a question word.
tips: Did you change anything in the policy?
Why did the rate go up in August?

listenings.text: I have told this story in three companies now, and it lands the same way every time. We launched the product in April and revenue rose in May. It rose again in June. Everybody was happy, and nobody asked a single question, including me. Then in August I saw the default rate climb, and the first thing I did was open the policy, not the model. That surprised my own team. But a model does what the rule tells it to do, and the rule had changed in March. Somebody had loosened it to let more customers in before the end of the quarter. I do not regret the launch. The product was right and it is still running today. What I regret is that nobody wrote down the reason for that change, so it took us three weeks to find something that should have taken ten minutes.

When a company calls me after a bad quarter, I ask two questions in the first ten minutes. Who changed the rule, and why. Almost everybody can answer the first half. Almost nobody can answer the second. And the change is never dramatic, that is the thing. Nobody wakes up and decides to take a huge risk. What happens is small: a team lets in customers with a shorter credit history, because the target for that quarter is close and this gets them there. It looks like nothing on the day it happens. Nine months later it is the whole story. So my advice is boring, and it works. Every change carries three things: a name, a date and a reason. Not a document, not a committee. Three lines, written by the person who made the call, on the day they made it.
